3: FROSCH Bravo! bravo! that was fine.
8: Every flea may it so befall!
11: Point your fingers and nip them all!
17: Hurrah for Freedom! Hurrah for wine!
22: I fain would drink with you, my glass to Freedom clinking, If ’twere a better wine that here I see you drinking.
32: Don’t let us hear that speech again!
44: Did I not fear the landlord might complain, I’d treat these worthy guests, with pleasure, To some from out our cellar’s treasure.
51: Just treat, and let the landlord me arraign!
58: And if the wine be good, our praises shall be ample. But do not give too very small a sample; For, if its quality I decide, With a good mouthful I must be supplied.
65: They’re from the Rhine! I guessed as much, before.
75: What shall therewith be done? You’ve not the casks already at the door?
86: Yonder, within the landlord’s box of tools, there’s one!
95: Now, give me of your taste some intimation.
99: How do you mean? Have you so many kinds?
104: The choice is free: make up your minds.
109: Aha! you lick your chops, from sheer anticipation.
115: Good! if I have the choice, so let the wine be Rhenish! Our Fatherland can best the sparkling cup replenish.
122: (boring a hole in the edge of the table, at the place where FROSCH sits)
128: Get me a little wax, to make the stoppers, quick!
135: Ah! I perceive a juggler’s trick.
143: Champagne shall be my wine, And let it sparkle fresh and fine!
151: (bores: in the meantime one has made the wax stoppers, and plugged the holes with them.)
159: What’s foreign one can’t always keep quite clear of, For good things, oft, are not so near; A German can’t endure the French to see or hear of, Yet drinks their wines with hearty cheer.
166: (as MEPHISTOPHELES approaches his seat) For me, I grant, sour wine is out of place; Fill up my glass with sweetest, will you?
174: Tokay shall flow at once, to fill you!
181: No—look me, Sirs, straight in the face! I see you have your fun at our expense.
189: O no! with gentlemen of such pretence, That were to venture far, indeed. Speak out, and make your choice with speed! With what a vintage can I serve you?
197: (After the holes have been bored and plugged)
206: Grapes the vine-stem bears, Horns the he-goat wears! The grapes are juicy, the vines are wood, The wooden table gives wine as good! Into the depths of Nature peer,— Only believe there’s a miracle here!
213: Now draw the stoppers, and drink your fill!
220: (as they draw out the stoppers, and the wine which has been desired flows into the glass of each)
226: O beautiful fountain, that flows at will!
229: But have a care that you nothing spill!
237: As ’twere five hundred hogs, we feel So cannibalic jolly!
243: See, now, the race is happy—it is free!
249: To leave them is my inclination.
252: Take notice, first! their bestiality Will make a brilliant demonstration.
258: (drinks carelessly: the wine spills upon the earth, and turns to flame)
262: Help! Fire! Help! Hell-fire is sent!
268: A bit of purgatory ’twas for this time, merely.
271: What mean you? Wait!—you’ll pay for’t dearly! You’ll know us, to your detriment.
277: Don’t try that game a second time upon us!
280: I think we’d better send him packing quietly.
286: What, Sir! you dare to make so free, And play your hocus-pocus on us!
295: Broomstick, you! You face it out, impertinent and heady?
300: Just wait! a shower of blows is ready.
303: (draws a stopper out of the table: fire flies in his face.) I burn! I burn!
313: ’Tis magic! Strike— The knave is outlawed! Cut him as you like! (They draw their knives, and rush upon MEPHISTOPHELES.)
321: False word and form of air, Change place, and sense ensnare! Be here—and there!
329: (They stand amazed and look at each other.)
332: Where am I? What a lovely land!
335: Vines? Can I trust my eyes?
343: Here, over this green arbor bending, See what a vine! what grapes depending!
349: (He takes SIEBEL by the nose: the others do the same reciprocally, and raise their knives.)
356: Loose, Error, from their eyes the band, And how the Devil jests, be now enlightened!
363: (He disappears with FAUST: the revellers start and separate.)
374: Was that your nose I tightened?
377: And yours that still I have in hand?
380: It was a blow that went through every limb! Give me a chair! I sink! my senses swim.
386: But what has happened, tell me now?
390: Where is he? If I catch the scoundrel hiding, He shall not leave alive, I vow.
398: I saw him with these eyes upon a wine-cask riding Out of the cellar-door, just now. Still in my feet the fright like lead is weighing. (He turns towards the table.) Why! If the fount of wine should still be playing?
406: ’Twas all deceit, and lying, false design!
413: And yet it seemed as I were drinking wine.
418: But with the grapes how was it, pray?
421:
Shall one believe no miracles, just say!

(Upon a low hearth stands a great caldron, under which a fire is burning. Various figures appear in the vapors which rise from the caldron. An ape sits beside it, skims it, and watches lest it boil over. The he-ape, with the young ones, sits near and warms himself. Ceiling and walls are covered with the most fantastic witch-implements.)

These crazy signs of witches’ craft repel me! I shall recover, dost thou tell me, Through this insane, chaotic play? From an old hag shall I demand assistance? And will her foul mess take away Full thirty years from my existence? Woe’s me, canst thou naught better find! Another baffled hope must be lamented: Has Nature, then, and has a noble mind Not any potent balsam yet invented?
430: Once more, my friend, thou talkest sensibly. There is, to make thee young, a simpler mode and apter; But in another book ’tis writ for thee, And is a most eccentric chapter.
437:
Yet will I know it.

Good! the method is revealed Without or gold or magic or physician. Betake thyself to yonder field, There hoe and dig, as thy condition; Restrain thyself, thy sense and will Within a narrow sphere to flourish; With unmixed food thy body nourish; Live with the ox as ox, and think it not a theft That thou manur’st the acre which thou reapest;— That, trust me, is the best mode left, Whereby for eighty years thy youth thou keepest!
443: I am not used to that; I cannot stoop to try it— To take the spade in hand, and ply it. The narrow being suits me not at all.
451: Then to thine aid the witch must call.
454:
Wherefore the hag, and her alone? Canst thou thyself not brew the potion?

That were a charming sport, I own: I’d build a thousand bridges meanwhile, I’ve a notion. Not Art and Science serve, alone; Patience must in the work be shown. Long is the calm brain active in creation; Time, only, strengthens the fine fermentation. And all, belonging thereunto, Is rare and strange, howe’er you take it: The Devil taught the thing, ’tis true, And yet the Devil cannot make it. (Perceiving the Animals) See, what a delicate race they be! That is the maid! the man is he! (To the Animals) It seems the mistress has gone away?
463: Carousing, to-day! Off and about, By the chimney out!
468: What time takes she for dissipating?
473: While we to warm our paws are waiting.
479: How findest thou the tender creatures?
482: Absurder than I ever yet did see.
486: Why, just such talk as this, for me, Is that which has the most attractive features!
492: But tell me now, ye cursed puppets, Why do ye stir the porridge so?
497: We’re cooking watery soup for beggars.
500: Then a great public you can show.
505: O cast thou the dice! Make me rich in a trice, Let me win in good season! Things are badly controlled, And had I but gold, So had I my reason.
512: How would the ape be sure his luck enhances. Could he but try the lottery’s chances!
518:
(In the meantime the young apes have been playing with a large ball, which they now roll forward.)

The world’s the ball: Doth rise and fall, And roll incessant: Like glass doth ring, A hollow thing,— How soon will’t spring, And drop, quiescent? Here bright it gleams, Here brighter seems: I live at present! Dear son, I say, Keep thou away! Thy doom is spoken! ’Tis made of clay, And will be broken.
528: Wert thou the thief, I’d know him and shame him.
533: (He runs to the SHE-APE, and lets her look through it.)
539: Look through the sieve! Know’st thou the thief, And darest not name him?
549: The fool knows it not! He knows not the pot, He knows not the kettle!
559: Take the brush here, at least, And sit down on the settle!
568:
(who during all this time has been standing before a mirror, now approaching and now retreating from it)

What do I see? What heavenly form revealed Shows through the glass from Magic’s fair dominions! O lend me, Love, the swiftest of thy pinions, And bear me to her beauteous field! Ah, if I leave this spot with fond designing, If I attempt to venture near, Dim, as through gathering mist, her charms appear!— A woman’s form, in beauty shining! Can woman, then, so lovely be? And must I find her body, there reclining, Of all the heavens the bright epitome? Can Earth with such a thing be mated?

Why, surely, if a God first plagues Himself six days, Then, self-contented, Bravo! says, Must something clever be created. This time, thine eyes be satiate! I’ll yet detect thy sweetheart and ensnare her, And blest is he, who has the lucky fate, Some day, as bridegroom, home to bear her.
575: (FAUST gazes continually in the mirror. MEPHISTOPHELES, stretching himself out on the settle, and playing with the brush, continues to speak.)
581: So sit I, like the King upon his throne: I hold the sceptre, here,—and lack the crown alone.
588: (who up to this time have been making all kinds of fantastic movements together bring a crown to MEPHISTOPHELES with great noise.)
594: O be thou so good With sweat and with blood The crown to belime!
600: (They handle the crown awkwardly and break it into two pieces, with which they spring around.)
606: ’Tis done, let it be! We speak and we see, We hear and we rhyme!
613: Woe’s me! I fear to lose my wits.
616: My own head, now, is really nigh to sinking.
622: If lucky our hits, And everything fits, ’Tis thoughts, and we’re thinking!
629: My bosom burns with that sweet vision; Let us, with speed, away from here!
636: One must, at least, make this admission— They’re poets, genuine and sincere.
641: (The caldron, which the SHE-APE has up to this time neglected to watch, begins to boil over: there ensues a great flame, which blazes out the chimney. The WITCH comes careering down through the flame, with terrible cries.)
650: Ow! ow! ow! ow! The damnéd beast—the curséd sow! To leave the kettle, and singe the Frau! Accurséd fere!
661: What is that here? Who are you here? What want you thus? Who sneaks to us? The fire-pain Burn bone and brain!
668: (She plunges the skimming-ladle into the caldron, and scatters flames towards FAUST, MEPHISTOPHELES, and the Animals. The Animals whimper.)
680: (reversing the brush, which he has been holding in his hand, and striding among the jars and glasses)
686: In two! in two! There lies the brew! There lies the glass! The joke will pass, As time, foul ass! To the singing of thy crew.
692:
(As the WITCH starts back, full of wrath and horror)

Ha! know’st thou me? Abomination, thou! Know’st thou, at last, thy Lord and Master? What hinders me from smiting now Thee and thy monkey-sprites with fell disaster? Hast for the scarlet coat no reverence? Dost recognize no more the tall cock’s-feather? Have I concealed this countenance?— Must tell my name, old face of leather?
698:
O pardon, Sir, the rough salute! Yet I perceive no cloven foot; And both your ravens, where are they now?

This time, I’ll let thee ’scape the debt; For since we two together met, ’Tis verily full many a day now. Culture, which smooth the whole world licks, Also unto the Devil sticks. The days of that old Northern phantom now are over: Where canst thou horns and tail and claws discover? And, as regards the foot, which I can’t spare, in truth, ’Twould only make the people shun me; Therefore I’ve worn, like many a spindly youth, False calves these many years upon me.
